summary:
FireBridge harmonises NASA's two wildfire-detecting satellite records, MODIS (since 2000, ~1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels), into one consistent 25-year fire record. Because VIIRS sees far more small fires, simply combining the records creates a false jump in fire activity in 2012, and MODIS retires in 2027, so a consistent record is needed now.

We processed 15.5 million NASA FIRMS detections: cleaning low-confidence and static heat sources, gridding them into half-degree daily cells, and learning a region-by-month correction from the years both sensors overlap. Tested on unseen years, this reduced the MODIS–VIIRS bias from −86% to −0.4%. On this record, an LSTM model forecasts fire activity and beats climatology and persistence baselines.

Our web app serves fire managers, land managers and residents with a global fire overview, a historical fire calendar, forecasts with uncertainty bands, and CSV/PDF downloads. We also built a tabletop "mini satellite" — two infrared sensors sweeping a 3D-printed terrain — to demonstrate the problem physically and show tracking continuing after MODIS is switched off.
details:
1. What the project does

Fire Bridge is a web application that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS active fire records into a single, comparable burning activity calendar from November 2000 to November 2026. Users select an area of interest (AOI) by clicking the map or entering coordinates, and can then explore:

  • A year-by-month burning activity heatmap, with anomalies relative to the historical median for the same month
  • Monthly activity summaries, peak months, and historical hotspot cells
  • 1 to 7 day fire-detection probabilities
  • A multi-month climatological outlook with risk levels
  • CSV downloads of the historical calendar and hotspot cells

2. How it works

Data and cleaning. We use the NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time (NRT) hotspots for MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP, and NOAA-20, totaling 15.5 million rows. Following the MODIS Active Fire User’s Guide, we keep nominal and high confidence detections, and following the FIRMS attribute tables, we keep only vegetation fires (type 0).

Gridding. Detections are aggregated into 0.5° cells by local solar day, following the gridded-aggregation practice of GFED5.

Harmonization. On the 2012-2021 overlap, we fit zero-intercept ratio-of-sums scalars for each region and month, scaling MODIS to a NOAA-20-equivalent count. The two VIIRS platforms are averaged, as in GFED5NRT.

Drift guard. MODIS orbit drift after 2021 would bias the calibration, so MODIS data after 2021 are excluded from fitting, and drift is measured directly from acq_time.

Validation. We hold out 2019-2021 and report Pearson r, slope, bias, and NRMSE, the metrics used by GFED5NRT.

Forecasting. Daily soft detection-probability labels come from VIIRS only, because the MODIS guide warns of sampling bias at scales below about 8 days. A single global LSTM (64 hidden units) is trained across all cells and benchmarked against climatology and persistence baselines using Brier skill score and PR-AUC.

Serving and updates. A FastAPI service handles model inference and a Spring Boot service exposes the API, falling back to precomputed results if the model service is offline. The FIRMS Area API feeds daily updates through the same feature code used in training.

3. Benefits

  • An unusual month reflects real fire behavior, not a change of instrument
  • Emergency responders, scientists, and land managers work from one shared record instead of each handling sensor differences separately
  • The interface distinguishes missing data, zero activity, incomplete months, and areas outside coverage, reducing misreading
  • Downloadable data plugs into existing analysis workflows

4. Expected impact

  • Earlier identification of critical fire periods, so monitoring resources can be allocated on evidence
  • Consistent long-term comparison of fire seasons and anomalies for researchers
  • A reproducible, literature-grounded approach that other regions and teams can reuse

5. Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet
  • Backend: Spring Boot (Java), Python FastAPI, LSTM model
  • Data: NASA FIRMS archive, NRT data, and Area API
  • Quality: unit tests, TypeScript type checking, linting, production builds
  • AI-assisted development: planning, architecture, implementation, testing, and debugging
  • Hardware: [TO FILL: training machine or GPU, deployment platform]

6. Innovation

  • Region-by-month ratio-of-sums cross-sensor calibration with an explicit MODIS drift exclusion
  • Local solar day rather than UTC dates, avoiding day-boundary count errors
  • Leave-one-year-out medians for anomalies, so an extreme year does not inflate its own baseline
  • VIIRS-only labels for forecasting, avoiding MODIS sampling bias
  • Honest forecast semantics: the output is a detection probability, not an ignition probability, and results are published alongside baselines
  • A fallback path when the model service is offline, with the data source labeled in the UI

7. Team considerations

  • Scientific correctness: sensor differences, orbit drift, sampling bias, and confidence classes are handled according to the literature
  • Honest uncertainty: the UI shows forecast limitations, model evaluation, and data coverage rather than presenting probabilities as certainties
  • Usability: incomplete months, out-of-coverage areas, accessibility, and chart scaling are handled explicitly
  • Robustness: a fallback mechanism, a stable API contract, and a repository pattern that isolates the frontend from backend formats
  • Responsible AI use: AI was a collaborative tool, not a decision-maker. Every change was reviewed and tested, and scientific meaning, API contracts, and interface decisions were confirmed by the team
